title: Genesis 20. The Cup Repeated.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 20. The Cup Repeated.
Abraham travels from there toward the land of the South.
He settles between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourns in Gerar.
And Abraham said of Sarah his wife: She is my sister.
The same lie.
The same words.
The same endangerment.
The man who was called righteous for believing God,
who was renamed father of nations,
who was sealed in flesh with circumcision, who interceded for Sodom,
who hosted God under a tree,
does the same thing he did in Egypt in chapter twelve.
Abimelech, king of Gerar, sends and takes Sarah.
The Cup of covenant, the woman through whom the promise must come,
the wife who was renamed for a mother of nations,
the womb that God Himself said would bear a son within the year,
is handed to another king.
Again.
The vessel that was filled with a promise from God is emptied by the fear of the man who received it.
Again.
God comes to Abimelech in a dream by night: Behold,
you are a dead man because of the woman you have taken.
She is a man's wife.
God does not come to Abraham.
God does not rebuke Abraham.
God goes to the man who took Sarah and warns him.
The Cup is preserved again, not by Abraham's integrity,
not by Abraham's prayer, not by Abraham's faith.
By God's intervention in a pagan king's dream.
The same God who struck Pharaoh's house with plagues in chapter twelve now closes every womb in Abimelech's household.
Abimelech has not come near her.
He argues: Lord, will You kill even a righteous nation?
Did he not say to me, She is my sister?
And she herself said, He is my brother.
In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands I have done this.
The pagan king pleads integrity.
The man who does not know God's covenant appeals to his own innocence.
And God acknowledges it.
Yes,
I know that in the integrity of your heart you have done this.
And I also withheld you from sinning against Me.
Therefore I did not let you touch her.
God confirms what Abimelech said.
The king of Gerar acted in innocence.
But God also reveals something deeper: He Himself prevented the sin.
I withheld you.
I did not let you touch her.
The Cup was protected not only from Abraham's fear but from Abimelech's ignorance.
God guarded the covenant through both the man who endangered it and the man who unknowingly held it.
Now therefore, restore the man's wife.
For he is a prophet, and he will pray for you,
and you will live.
If you do not restore her, know that you shall surely die,
you and all that are yours.
Abraham is called a prophet.
The first time the word appears in Scripture.
Not in a moment of glory.
Not on a mountain.
Not at an altar.
In the moment of his failure.
The man who just sold his wife is called God's prophet,
the one who will pray for the king he deceived.
The Cup that was endangered by the vessel is now the instrument through which the vessel becomes a blessing to the one it endangered.
Abimelech rises early in the morning.
He calls his servants.
He tells them everything.
The men are very afraid.
Then he calls Abraham: What have you done to us?
How have I sinned against you,
that you have brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin?
You have done to me things that ought not to be done.
For the second time in Genesis,
a pagan king rebukes the man God called.
Pharaoh said it in chapter twelve: What is this you have done?
Abimelech says it here: What have you done to us?
The vessel of the covenant is corrected by kings who do not carry the covenant.
Abimelech asks: What did you see that you did this thing?
Abraham answers: Because I thought,
Surely the fear of God is not in this place,
and they will kill me for my wife's sake.
Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father,
but not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife.
When God caused me to wander from my father's house,
I said to her: This is the kindness you shall show me.
At every place we go, say of me, He is my brother.
Abraham's defense is not defense.
It is confession.
He assumed the worst.
He assumed Gerar had no fear of God.
And so he lied, preemptively, systematically,
from the day he left his father's house.
This was not a one-time failure in Egypt.
This was a plan.
A strategy.
A pattern that Abraham and Sarah agreed to before the journey even began.
Every place they went, she would say: He is my brother.
The man who believed God for offspring as countless as the stars could not believe God for safety in a foreign city.
The faith that could hold the promise of a son could not hold the hand of a wife.
The Cup that was received by faith was repeatedly endangered by fear.
Abimelech takes sheep, cattle, male servants, female servants,
and gives them to Abraham.
He restores Sarah.
He says: My land is before you.
Dwell where it pleases you.
To Sarah he says:
I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver.
It is a covering of the eyes for you and for all who are with you.
You are righted.
The king who was wronged pays the man who wronged him.
The one who was deceived gives gifts to the deceiver.
And the silver, a thousand pieces,
is called a covering of the eyes.
The same word for covering is used in Genesis elsewhere for garments and concealment.
Abimelech covers what Abraham exposed.
The pagan king restores what the prophet endangered.
Abraham prays to God.
God heals Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants.
They bear children,
for the Lord had closed all the wombs of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah,
Abraham's wife.
The man whose own wife was barren prays for the wombs of another man's household.
The prophet whose wife cannot conceive intercedes for the wombs that God closed.
And they open.
The Cup that was nearly lost is now the instrument of healing.
The vessel that endangered the covenant becomes the vessel through which the covenant's God restores life.
The Cup repeated.
The same crack in the same vessel.
The same fear.
The same lie.
The same God who covers it.
What was a one-time failure in chapter twelve is revealed here as a lifelong pattern,
a strategy agreed to before the calling, before the covenant,
before the altar at Shechem.
Abraham has been doing this since he left Ur.
And yet.
The covenant stands.
The promise holds.
Sarah is returned.
The wombs of Gerar are opened.
The man who fumbled is called a prophet.
The God who was not consulted in the arrangement with Hagar is the God who intervenes in the dream of a king who did not know he was touching a covenant.
The Cup is not preserved by the vessel's strength.
It never has been.
From the garden to the ark to Gerar,
the Cup holds because the hand that fills it does not let go.
The vessel cracks in the same place, the same way, every time.
And the Cup is still full.
Sarah is back.
The promise of a son is still spoken.
The next chapter will hold what this chapter almost lost.
But first, the silence.
The man who lied and the king who paid and the woman who was taken and the God who closed wombs and opened them again.
All of them standing in Gerar.
All of them aware, now,
that the woman in the tent is not a sister.
She is a wife.
And she carries something neither of them can see.
